Allah, glory be to Him, knew, before His servants came into existence, their states, what they would do, and where they would end. Then He brought them out into this abode so that what He knew about them would become manifest, as He had known it. He tested them with commands and prohibitions, with good and evil, by manifesting what He knew. They therefore deserved praise and blame, reward and punishment, on account of the deeds and attributes that arose in them, which corresponded to His prior knowledge. They would not have deserved that while those deeds were still in His knowledge before they performed them. He sent His messengers, revealed His books, and legislated His laws as a warning to them and as an establishment of proof against them, lest they say: "Why do You punish us for Your knowledge of us? This is not within our acquisition or our capacity." So when His knowledge of them became manifest through their actions, punishment came upon what He knew, which the trial and the examination had made evident.

Just as He tested them through His command and prohibition, He tested them through what He made attractive to them of this world and through the desires He placed in them. The former is His trial through His legislation and command, and the latter is a trial through His decree and destiny. He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾. He also said: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, while His Throne was upon the water﴾. In this verse He informs that He created the heavens and the earth in order to test His servants by His command and prohibition. This is part of the truth by which He created His creation. In the verse before it, He informed that He created death and life in order to test them as well. He gave them life to test them by His command and prohibition, and He decreed death for them, through which they would attain the consequence of that test, namely reward and punishment. And indeed, He informed in the first verse that He made what is on the earth an adornment to test them with it, to see which of them prefers what is with Him, and He tested some of them by means of others. Jinn and humans are each tested by the other. So the trial of Adam made manifest what He knew of him, and the trial of Iblis made manifest what He knew of him. For this reason He said to the angels: ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾. This trial continued among the descendants until the Day of Resurrection. He tested the prophets through their peoples, and He tested their peoples through them. He said to His servant, messenger and intimate friend: "Indeed, I will test you, and you will be tested by means of you." He said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned﴾. He said: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾.

In the authentic hadith: "Three men whom Allah wished to test: a leper, a bald man, and a blind man. Allah manifested through the trial their true states, which had been in His knowledge before He created them. As for the blind man, he acknowledged Allah's favour upon him, that he had been a blind, poor man, and Allah gave him sight and wealth, and he gave to the beggar what he asked of him, out of gratitude to Allah. As for the leper and the bald man, both of them denied what they had been before, of bad condition and poverty, and when speaking of their wealth, one said: 'I have only inherited it from one great man after another.'" This is the state of most people, who do not acknowledge what they were at first of deficiency, ignorance, poverty and sins, and that Allah, glory be to Him, moved them from that to the opposite of what they had been, and bestowed that blessing upon them. For this reason, He draws the human being's attention to the origin of his creation, from a weak fluid, a contemptible water, and then moves him through the stages and phases of his creation, from one state to another, until He made him a complete human who hears, sees, speaks, articulates, grasps and knows. Yet he forgets his origin and beginning and how he once was, and does not acknowledge the blessings of his Lord upon him, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Does every one of them aspire to enter a garden of bliss? No! Indeed, We created them from that which they know﴾.

Ibn al-Qayyim (Tafsir Ibn al-Qayyim) on Surah 11, verses 9–10:

He censured him for despair and disbelief when tested by affliction, and for exultation and boasting when tested by blessings, and in exchange (for that) praise and thanks to God and commendation of Him when He removed the affliction from him. (The verse says) "Evil has departed from me," and had he said, "God has removed the evils from me by His mercy," he would not have been censured for that; rather, he would have been praised for it. But he was heedless of the Benefactor who removed them and attributed the departure to them (the evils), and he exulted and boasted. So when God, glory be to Him, knows this from a servant's heart, that is among the greatest causes of his abandonment and of God leaving him alone, for his (the servant's) place is not suited to receive the complete and absolute blessing. As God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and the dumb who do not reason. And if God had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were refusing.﴾

So He, glory be to Him, informed that their place does not accept His blessing, and along with their non-acceptance, there is another obstacle in them that prevents its reaching them: their turning away and their aversion once they recognize it and ascertain it.

(Section)

Wealth, if it does not benefit its owner, will inevitably harm him. The same is true of knowledge, dominion, and power: if these do not benefit their possessor, they harm him. For these things are means (wasa'il, sing. wasilah, "means") to ends that one reaches through them, whether for good or for evil. If they are left idle, not employed as means to praiseworthy aims and ends, they are employed as means to their opposites.

The most profitable of people, then, are those who make these things means to God and the Last Abode, and this is what benefits them in their livelihood and their return. The greatest losers are those who employ them to gratify their desires and attain their immediate aims, and so they lose both this world and the next. Such a person has not made the means into ends; had he done so, he would still have been a loser, but he has made them means to the very opposite of what they were made for. He is like one who uses the causes of pleasure to reach the greatest of pains and their sources.

Thus the divisions are four, with no fifth:

The first: one who neglects the causes and turns away from them.

The second: one who is absorbed in them, stopping at their gathering and acquisition.

The third: one who uses them to reach what harms him and does not benefit him in his livelihood or his return. These three are in loss.

The fourth: one who uses them to reach what benefits him in his livelihood and his return. He is the winner. God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein. Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire; what they did therein will be voided, and what they used to do will be worthless.﴾

The meaning of this verse has been unclear to many people, for they understood from it that whoever has a desire for this world and its adornment faces this threat. Then they differed about its meaning. A group, including Ibn 'Abbas, said: whoever desires the hastening of this world does not believe in the Resurrection, reward, or punishment. They said the verse concerns the disbelievers specifically, according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Qatadah said: whoever has the world as his concern, his preoccupation, his intention and his pursuit, God will recompense him in this world for his good deeds, and then he will arrive at the Hereafter with no good deed for which he can be rewarded.

As for the believer, he is recompensed in this world for his good deeds and is rewarded for them in the Hereafter.

These scholars said: the verse concerns the disbelievers, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire; what they did therein will be voided, and what they used to do will be worthless.﴾ They said: the believer is one who desires both this world and the Hereafter, whereas one whose desire is confined to this world is not a believer.

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said, in the narration of Abu Salih from him: it was revealed concerning the People of the Qiblah (ahl al-qiblah, i.e., Muslims).

Mujahid said: they are the people of riya' (showing off).

Al-Dahhak said: whoever performs a righteous deed among the people of faith without piety, his reward for that deed is hastened to him in this world.

Al-Farra' chose this view and said: whoever among the People of the Qiblah intends by his deed the reward of this world, his reward is hastened to him and is not diminished.

This view is more preponderant. The meaning of the verse on this view is: whoever intends by his deed the life of this world and its adornment. Such a person cannot be a believer at all, for the disobedient and the wicked, however far they go in disobedience and sin, are still driven by what moves them to perform acts of righteousness for God, and they intend by those acts of righteousness the face of God, even if they also commit acts of disobedience.

As for one who does not intend by his deed the face of God, but intends only this world and its adornment, he does not enter the circle of the people of faith. This is what Mu'awiyah understood from the verse, and he cited it as evidence for the hadith of Abu Hurayrah narrated by Muslim in his Sahih, concerning the three who will be the first whom the Fire is kindled for on the Day of Resurrection: the reciter who recited the Qur'an so that it would be said, "So-and-so is a reciter"; the almsgiver who spent his wealth so that it would be said, "So-and-so is generous"; and the warrior who was killed in jihad so that it would be said, "He is brave."

Just as the best of God's creation are the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous, the worst of creation is one who imitates them without being among them. Whoever imitates the people of sincerity and truthfulness while being a show-off is like one who imitates the prophets while being a liar.

Those who oppose revelation with their own reasoning have combined three things: lying about God, turning people away from the path of God, and seeking to make it crooked.

As for lying about God, they negate from Him the attributes of perfection that He affirmed for Himself, and they describe Him with what He did not describe Himself with.

As for their turning people away from His path and seeking to make it crooked, they gave people to understand, and even stated plainly to them, that the words of God and His Messenger are mere verbal surfaces that yield neither knowledge nor certainty, and that reason opposes them, so reason must be given precedence over them.

And what crookedness is greater than the crookedness of opposing clear reason? God has described His Book as ﴿without any crookedness﴾. There is no doubt that God is the Truthful in this, and that they are the liars.

If you say: ﴿yabghūnahā﴾ is transitive to one object, so what is the basis for ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ being in the accusative?

It is said: there are several explanations.

The first: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning they seek it while it is crooked, not while it is straight; the sense is that they seek crookedness for it.

The second: ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ is the object of ﴿yabghūnahā﴾ with the preposition removed, meaning they seek for it crookedness, which they attribute to it and describe it with.

Better than both is that ﴿yabghūnahā﴾ is taken to include the meaning of ﴿yuʿawwijūnahā﴾ (they make it crooked), so that ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ is an accusative of the verbal noun, and the verb "seeking" (al-baghy) indicates the pursuit and seeking of that.

As for the meaning of ﴿yasūmūnahā﴾ and ﴿yu'awwilūnahā﴾ [and the rest]...

In every case, the path of God is His guidance, and His Book is the guide to the most upright way and the most direct road. Whoever claims that reason opposes it has sought to make it crooked and has called people to turn away from it. Whoever has knowledge of sound reasoning knows that crookedness is in the speech of these crooked people, who have deviated from the Path, strayed from the way of rectitude, turned away from the signs of God, and who speak falsehood and false propositions, who persist in their error and waver in their doubt, and who oppose clear reason and sound revelation alike.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers." Unquestionably, they are the corrupters, but they do not perceive (11) And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?" Unquestionably, they are the foolish, but they do not know (13) And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking." (14) Allah mocks them and extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly (15)﴾.

Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 20:

He negated from them the ability to hear, despite the soundness and integrity of their senses. Rather, because of their extreme hatred and aversion towards him and his speech, they became like one who is unable to hear him or see him. This is a well-known usage among the elite and the common people: they say, "I cannot bear to look at so-and-so," and "I cannot stand to hear his words," on account of their hatred and aversion towards him.

Some of the Jabriyya (Determinists) cite this verse and similar verses in support of their doctrine, but there is no proof in them. The intended meaning is not the negation of hearing and sight by which the proof is established, which is certainly not the case. Rather, what is intended is the negation of the hearing whose benefit and fruit follow from it. Divine decree is true, but it is obligatory to place the Qur'an in its proper positions, to put the verses in their right places, and to follow the truth wherever it is found. Likewise, in such a case, if a person does not grasp the address, he is not excused by this, because the defect lies with him; he is like one who plugs his ears when addressed and so does not hear, and this is not an excuse for him.

The khabt in its original linguistic sense is a low-lying place on the ground, and Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah explained the word "al-mukhbitīn" (the humble ones) with this meaning, and both said: they are the humble ones. Mujahid said:

The mukhbit: the one who is at peace with/settled upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He said: al-khabt is the level, settled place of the ground. Al-Akhfash said:

They are the submissive ones (al-khāshiʿūn).

Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: they are those who pray sincerely (al-muṣallūn al-mukhliṣūn).

Al-Kalbi said: they are those whose hearts are tender. ʿAmr ibn Aws said: they are those who do not wrong others, and when they are wronged, they do not seek retribution.

These statements all revolve around two meanings: humility, and tranquil settling upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. For this reason the verb is followed by "ilā" (to) by way of taḍmīn (verb-complementation), carrying the sense of tranquility (ṭumaʾnīnah), turning back in repentance (inābah), and settling upon Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 24:

Indeed, He (glorified is He) mentioned the disbelievers and described them as being unable to hear and not seeing. Then He mentioned the believers and described them with faith, righteous deeds, and humble submission (ikhbat) to their Lord. Thus He described them with servitude (ubudiyyah) of the outward and the inward. He made one of the two groups like the blind and the deaf, in that his heart was blind to seeing the truth and deaf to hearing it. So He likened him to one whose sight is blind to seeing things and whose hearing is deaf to hearing sounds. The other group is one whose heart sees and whose hearing is attentive, like one whose eye sees and whose ear hears. Thus the verse includes two analogies (qiyasayn) and two illustrations (tamthilayn) for the two groups. Then He negated equality between the two groups with His saying: ﴿Are the two equal in comparison?﴾ [Hud: 24]..

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 27:

The Almighty's saying, reporting about the disbelievers that they said: ﴿We see you only as a human being like ourselves﴾.

They took into consideration the mere form of humanity and the similarity of kind in it, and they used this as evidence that the ruling for one of the two similar things is the ruling for the other. Just as we cannot be messengers, so neither can you; so if we are equal in this similarity, then you are like us, with no superiority over us. This is among the most invalid analogies (qiyas), for the actual state of affairs, with its particularization and preference, and its making some of this species noble and some base, some subordinate and some superior, some a king and some a commoner, refutes this analogy. As He, glorified is He, pointed out in His saying: ﴿Do they apportion the mercy of your Lord? We have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We have raised some of them above others in degrees, that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32].

The messengers answered this question with their saying: ﴿We are only human beings like you, but Allah bestows His favor upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [Ibrahim: 11]. And Allah, glorified is He, answered it with His saying: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. Likewise is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the eminent ones of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given luxury in the life of this world, said: "This is not but a human being like you. He eats from what you eat and drinks from what you drink"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 33], and ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, indeed you would then be losers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 34]. They regarded equality in humanity, and what is not among its distinctive features such as eating and drinking, as sufficient, and this is merely an analogy of resemblance and a formal grouping. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿That was because their messengers came to them with clear proofs, and they said: "Shall mere humans guide us?"﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6].

Among this is the polytheists' analogy of usury (riba) to sale on the basis of mere formal resemblance, and among it is their analogy of carrion (maytah) to slaughtered animals regarding the permissibility of eating, on the basis of mere resemblance.

In sum, this kind of analogy has not come in the Qur'an except rejected and blamed.

[Section: The Station of Secrecy]

[The Reality of Secrecy]

The author of al-Manazil said:

"The chapter on secrecy. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah knows best what is in their souls.﴾"

The people of secrecy are the hidden ones (al-akhfiya') concerning whom a report has been transmitted.

As for his citing the verse, its point is this: the followers of the Messengers who believed them and preferred Allah and the Last Abode over their own people and companions, Allah has deposited in their hearts a secret of the secrets of His knowledge, His love, and faith in Him, which was hidden from the enemies of the Messengers. They looked at their outward appearance and were blind to their inner realities, so they belittled and despised them, and said to the Messenger: "Drive these away from you, so that we may come to you and listen to you." They also said: ﴿Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ [al-An'am: 53]. Then Noah, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿I do not say to you that with me are the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel, nor do I say to those whom your eyes look down upon that Allah will never give them any good. Allah knows best what is in their souls. Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾ [Hud: 31]

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: if you claim that they only followed me in superficial and outward judgement, then it is not incumbent upon me to know what is in their souls. Whenever I see one who affirms the oneness of Allah, I act upon his outward state and refer the knowledge of what is in their souls to Allah. This is a good meaning.

What appears from the verse is that Allah knows what is in their souls, since He qualified them to accept His religion and His monotheism and to affirm His messengers. Allah, glorified and exalted, is All-Knowing, All-Wise, who places bounty in its proper place. This verse is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We tried some of them through others, that they might say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?" Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ [al-An'am: 53]. They denied that Allah, glorified is He, would qualify them for guidance and truth while withholding it from the leaders of the disbelievers and the people of might and wealth among them, as though they inferred the bounty of the Hereafter from the bounty of this world. So Allah, glorified is He, informed that He knows best whom to qualify for that, owing to a secret with Him: from knowing the value of the blessing, seeing it as pure grace from the Benefactor, loving Him and thanking Him for it. And his saying in another hadith, when "a man passed by him, and he said: 'What do you say about this one?' They said: 'He is worthy that if he intercedes he be interceded for, if he proposes marriage he be married, and if he speaks he be listened to.' Then another man passed by him, and he said: 'What do you say about this one?' They said: 'This one is worthy that if he intercedes he not be interceded for, if he proposes he not be married, and if he speaks he not be listened to.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This one is better than a world full of the likes of this one.'"

[Section: The Station of Secrecy]

[The Reality of Secrecy]

The author of al-Manazil said:

"The chapter on secrecy. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah knows best what is in their souls.﴾"

The people of secrecy are the hidden ones (al-akhfiya') concerning whom a report has been transmitted.

As for his citing the verse, its point is this: the followers of the Messengers who believed them and preferred Allah and the Last Abode over their own people and companions, Allah has deposited in their hearts a secret of the secrets of His knowledge, His love, and faith in Him, which was hidden from the enemies of the Messengers. They looked at their outward appearance and were blind to their inner realities, so they belittled and despised them, and said to the Messenger: "Drive these away from you, so that we may come to you and listen to you." They also said: ﴿Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ [al-An'am: 53]. Then Noah, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿I do not say to you that with me are the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel, nor do I say to those whom your eyes look down upon that Allah will never give them any good. Allah knows best what is in their souls. Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾ [Hud: 31]

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: if you claim that they only followed me in superficial and outward judgement, then it is not incumbent upon me to know what is in their souls. Whenever I see one who affirms the oneness of Allah, I act upon his outward state and refer the knowledge of what is in their souls to Allah. This is a good meaning.

What appears from the verse is that Allah knows what is in their souls, since He qualified them to accept His religion and His monotheism and to affirm His messengers. Allah, glorified and exalted, is All-Knowing, All-Wise, who places bounty in its proper place. This verse is similar to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We tried some of them through others, that they might say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?" Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ [al-An'am: 53]. They denied that Allah, glorified is He, would qualify them for guidance and truth while withholding it from the leaders of the disbelievers and the people of might and wealth among them, as though they inferred the bounty of the Hereafter from the bounty of this world. So Allah, glorified is He, informed that He knows best whom to qualify for that, owing to a secret with Him: from knowing the value of the blessing, seeing it as pure grace from the Benefactor, loving Him and thanking Him for it. Not everyone has this secret with Him. Thus not everyone is qualified for this bounty.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This one is better than a world full of the likes of this one.'"

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 32:

God placed in the hearts of the followers of His messengers a secret of the secrets of His knowledge and love, and faith in Him is hidden from the enemies of the messengers. They looked at their outward appearance and were blind to their inner reality, so they belittled and despised them, and said to the Messenger: "Send these away until we come to you and hear from you." And they said: ﴿Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favor from among us?﴾ Then Nuh said to his people: ﴿And I do not say to you that with me are the treasuries of God, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel, nor do I say to those whom your eyes look down upon that God will never give them any good. God is most knowing of what is within their souls.﴾

Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: The meaning is: if you claim that they followed me based on superficial and apparent opinion, then it is not incumbent upon me to know what is in their souls. So when I see someone who affirms the oneness of God, I act upon his outward state and I refer the knowledge of what is in their souls back to God. And this is a good meaning.

What appears from the verse is that God knows what is in their souls, since He qualified them to accept His religion, His monotheism, and the confirmation of His messengers, and God, glorified and exalted is He, is Wise, placing bounty in its proper places.

This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿And thus We tested some of them by means of others, that they might say: "Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favor from among us?" Is God not most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾

They denied that God, glorified is He, had qualified them for guidance and truth, while He withheld it from the leaders of the disbelievers and their people of power and wealth. It was as if they inferred the bounty of the Hereafter from the bounty of this world. So He, glorified is He, informed that He is most knowing of who is qualified for that, due to a secret He has in knowing the worth of blessing and seeing it as pure grace of the Benefactor, love for Him, and gratitude for it. Not everyone possesses this secret, so this bounty is not conferred on everyone.

(Fāʼida)

On the placing of a conditional upon conditionals, which takes several forms:

First: "If you go out and wear [it], then you are divorced." He does not break the oath except by both of them, however they occur.

Second: "If you wear [it] and then go out, he does not break the oath except by going out after wearing."

Third: "If you wear [it] then go out, he does not break the oath except by her going out after her wearing it, not with it, and it being delayed. This is built on the apparent wording; as for his intention, it is taken into account and one does not look beyond this."

Fourth: "If you go out, not if you wear [it]": he breaks the oath by going out alone and does not break it by wearing. This conditional may bear two meanings:

The first: that going out is made the condition, and wearing is left as a condition, its ruling being what we have mentioned.

The second: that going out without wearing is made the condition, so he does not break the oath by going out while wearing it. The meaning is: "If you go out not wearing it, or not wearing her [garment]", so if she goes out wearing it, he does not break the oath.

Fifth: "If you go out, but rather if you wear [it]": he does not break the oath except by wearing, not by going out. This conditional may also bear two meanings:

The first: this.

The second: that each of them is a condition, so he breaks the oath by whichever occurs, and the "but rather" (iḍrāb) is an iḍrāb of restriction, not of cancellation. It is as if he says: "I do not restrict the first alone to being the condition; rather, whichever of them occurs, it is a condition." On the first interpretation, the iḍrāb is one of cancellation and reversal; on the second, it is an iḍrāb of restriction and singling out.

Sixth: "If you go out or if you wear [it]": he breaks the oath by whichever occurs.

Seventh: "If you wear [it], but if you go out": the second condition cancels the first by "but" (lākin), since it is for correction.

Eighth: this is the most problematic of them: "If you wear [it] if you go out." This is the case of a conditional placed upon a conditional (dukhūl al-sharṭ ʿalā al-sharṭ). The conditioning here may bear two meanings:

The first: that each of them is made an independent condition, so it is like something joined by "and" (wa), and there is no difficulty.

The second: that one of them is made a condition for the other. The jurists differed on the ruling in this case. The companions of Mālik said: it is a conditioning of a conditioning (taʿlīq li-l-taʿlīq); in this statement there are two conditionings:

One: "If you wear [it], then you are divorced," and then this conditioned sentence is itself conditioned on going out. So it is as if he said: the condition for this conditioning to take effect is going out. On this basis, he does not break the oath until going out occurs after wearing. Among those who stated this explicitly is Ibn Shāsh in al-Jawāhir. Abū Isḥāq said in al-Muhadhdhab, having illustrated the case: "If I speak to Zayd, if I enter the house, then you are divorced. Then if I speak to Zayd, you are divorced; but if I speak to Zayd first and then enter the house, you are not divorced, because he made entering the house a condition on speaking to Zayd, so it must be placed before it." This is the reverse of the Mālikī view. Abū al-Maʿālī preferred the Mālikī view in his Nihāya.

This conditioning occurs in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in several places:

First: His saying, relating from Noah: ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you, if I wish to advise you, if Allah wishes to lead you astray﴾.

This clearly shows that the second condition is a condition within the first condition. The meaning is: if Allah wishes to lead you astray, my counsel will not benefit you, if I wish it. This supports the correctness of what Shaykh Abū Isḥāq said.

Second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her, [she is] exclusively for you﴾.

They said: this verse clearly supports the Mālikī view, because the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ wishing comes after her gift, since her gift runs in the place of acceptance in this contract, while the offer is her gift.

A parallel to this is one saying: "If he gives me something, if I wish to accept it, I take it." The wish to accept comes after the gift, so it is not a condition on it. The earlier scholars said: it is possible that the wish is that of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; when the woman understood that from him, she gave herself to him, so it is like the first verse.

This is not correct, and the narrative rejects it: the woman stood up and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have given myself to you," and he looked at her intently and considered her, then did not marry her, and someone else married her.

Third: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then why, if you are not under judgment, do you not return it, if you are truthful?﴾

The meaning: "Then why do you not return it," i.e., send back the soul when it reaches the throat, "if you are not indebted, subjected, owned, if you are truthful." Here the second is a condition on the first, and the meaning is: if you are truthful in your saying, then why do you not return it, if you are not indebted? This is shown by the verse of the poet which ʿAbd Allah ibn Mālik recited:

*If you seek help from us, if you are startled and find*
*from us strongholds of honour, which generosity has adorned.*

It is known that seeking help occurs only after alarm, so the alarm is a condition on it.

From this is the saying of al-Duraydī:

*So if I stumble after it, if my soul is detached from these, then say: "No, may you not be exalted."*

It is known that stumbling a second time occurs only after escaping the first, so "if my soul is detached" is a condition on the second condition. On this basis, when you mention the two conditions and then give the answer, the answer belongs to the first alone, and the second runs alongside it in the manner of a supplement and completion, like the circumstantial clause and other supplements. This is what Ibn Mālik said.

Better than this is to say: the statement is not two conditions requiring two answers, but one condition and one conditioning, in which a particular restriction was considered in one part, made a condition within it, and the answer belongs to the restricted condition. Thus it is an answer to both together by this consideration. Its clarification: when you say, "If I speak to Zayd, if I see him, then you are divorced," you have made the divorce the consequence of a speaking restricted by seeing, not of unrestricted speaking. It is as if he said: "If I speak to him while looking at him, then you are divorced." This clarifies for you the core of the issue and removes its difficulty entirely. And success is from Allah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 43:

When he mentioned "the protector" (al-'asim), the context called for a "protected one" (ma'sum) to be understood. It is as if it were said: "No one is protected today from His command except the one upon whom He has mercy." For when He said, ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah﴾,

the mind remained seeking the protected one, so it is as if it were asked: "Who then is protected?" It was answered: "None is protected except by the mercy of Allah." This expression, by its brevity, its majesty and its eloquence, indicates the negation of every protector other than Him, and the negation of every protected one other than the one upon whom Allah has mercy. Thus the exception indicates two matters: who is the protected one, and who is the Protector, namely the One who possesses mercy. This is among the most eloquent, most expressive and most concise of speech, and one should not give attention to what has been said about the verse after this. They have stated three other opinions:

The first: that 'asim here means ma'sum (protected), as in "ma' dafiq" (a gushing water) and "'isha radiya" (a pleasing life). The meaning would be: "No one is protected except by the mercy of Allah." This is corrupt, because each of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) and the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul) is coined for its own specific meaning, so the other does not share it. Al-ma' al-dafiq does not mean "the one being poured," but is an active form in its proper sense, as one says "ma' jari" (flowing water), so "dafiq" is like "jari." What requires the cold (al-takhlif al-barid) is... As for "'isha radiya," according to Sibawayh it is of the relative form (al-nasab), like "tamir" (possessing dates) and "laban" (possessing milk), meaning "one possessing satisfaction"; and according to others it is like "nahar sa'im" (a day of fasting) and "layl qa'im" (a night of standing prayer), in the sense of intensification.

The second opinion: that man rahima (whoever has mercy) is an active form, not a passive one, and the meaning is: "None protects today from the command of Allah except the one who shows mercy." Thus it is an exception of an agent from an agent. Although this is less burdened with artificiality, it is also very weak, and the grandeur and eloquence of the speech reject it at first glance.

The third opinion: that the speech contains an elided genitive construction (mudaf mahdhuf), with the genitive noun taking its place, and the estimated meaning is: "No protected protector today from the command of Allah except one upon whom Allah has mercy." This is among the most objectionable of opinions and the most contrary to eloquence and rhetoric; if it were stated explicitly, it would be a matter for seeking forgiveness.

(Benefit)

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, used to write on his forehead: ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold," and the water subsided and the matter was decided﴾.

I heard him say: "I wrote it for more than one person and they recovered." Then he said: "It is not permissible to write it with the blood of one with a nosebleed, as the ignorant do, for blood is impure, and it is not permissible to write the speech of Allah the Exalted with it."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 46:

Some scholars have argued from the fact that Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, said to Noah concerning his son: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, he is [one whose] work is other than righteous﴾.

So He removed him from being of his family because of his disbelief (shirk), and thus it is known that the family (āl) of the Messenger ﷺ are his followers.

Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him) gave a good answer to this, namely that the meaning is: "He is not of your family whom We commanded you to carry and whose salvation We promised you," because Allah, glorified is He, said to him before that: ﴿Carry upon it two of each pair, and your family, except those against whom the word has already preceded﴾.

So his son was not among the family whose salvation He had guaranteed.

I say: What confirms the correctness of this is that the context of the verse indicates that those who believed in him were a category distinct from his family, those who are his family, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Carry upon it of each pair two, and your family, except those against whom the word has preceded, and those who believed﴾.

So ﴿those who believed﴾ is conjoined to the object of "carry," and they are the family, and the two of each pair.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 11, verses 53–55:

Indeed, among the most hidden of the signs of the Messengers are the signs of Hud, peace be upon him, to the extent that his people said to him: ﴿O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof﴾.

Yet his proof is among the most manifest of proofs, and he pointed to it with his words: ﴿Indeed, I call Allah to witness, and you bear witness, that I am free from what you associate with Him, besides Him. So plot against me all together, then give me no respite. Indeed, I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 54–56]. This is among the greatest of signs: that a single man addresses a mighty nation with this address, neither anxious nor fearful, nor feeble, but confident in what he has said, resolute in it, calling Allah first to witness his innocence from their religion and from what they are upon, with the witnessing of one who trusts in Him, relies upon Him, and informs his people that He is his Protector and Helper, and that He will not give them power over him.

Then he called them to witness, openly declaring his opposition to them, that he is free from their religion and their gods, to which they show loyalty and enmity, and for whose support they expend their lives and their wealth.

Then he confirmed this for them by making light of them, belittling them and despising them, and [declared] that even if they all gathered together in his plot, and to satisfy their rage against him, and then dealt with him without giving him any respite, [he would still not be harmed]. Implicit in this is that they are weaker, more incapable and less than that, and that if you were to attempt it, you would turn back in your rage, humiliated and forsaken.

Then he established his call in the finest manner, and made clear that his Lord and their Lord, in whose hand their forelocks are, is the One who is his Protector and Trustee, who undertakes his victory and support, and that He is upon a straight path. He does not forsake whoever puts his trust in Him and believes in Him, nor does He let His enemies rejoice over him, nor is He with them against him, for His straight path upon which He is, in His speech and His action, prevents this and refuses it.

Under this address is also [the meaning] that from His straight path is that He takes vengeance upon those who have departed from it and acted contrary to it, and brings down His might upon them. For the straight path is the justice upon which the Lord, exalted is He, is; and from it is His vengeance upon the people of polytheism and transgression, and His support of His allies and Messengers against their enemies, and that He removes them and replaces them with other people, and this does Him no harm whatsoever; and that He, glorified is He, is the One who watches over everything, in preservation, care, governance and enumeration.

What sign, proof and evidence is finer than the signs of the Prophets and their proofs and evidences? They are a testimony from Allah, glorified is He, for them, which He made clear to His servants to the utmost clarity, and manifested to them to the utmost manifestation through His word and His deed. And in the authentic [collection], from him (ﷺ), he said: "There is no Prophet among the Prophets except that he was given signs by which mankind believed, and what I was given was a revelation which Allah revealed to me; so I hope that I will be the one with the most followers on the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 56:

So His saying, ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ [Hud: 56] is like His saying, "My forelock is in Your hand." And His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56] is like His saying, "Just is Your judgment."

The first refers to His dominion, and the second to His praiseworthiness. He, glorified is He, possesses the dominion and possesses the praise. His being on a straight path requires that He says only the truth, commands only justice, and does only what is beneficial, merciful, wise and just. He is upon the truth in His sayings and His actions. He does not judge a servant in a way that would be unjust to him, nor does He seize him for other than his sin, nor does He diminish any of his good deeds, nor does He burden him with the evil deeds of others which he did not commit nor was the cause of, nor does He hold anyone accountable for another's sin, nor does He ever do what is not praiseworthy, nor what does not bring praise to Him, and in which there are not good outcomes and desired ends for Him. For His being on a straight path rejects all of that.

Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56], means: Indeed my Lord is on the way of truth, rewarding the good-doer among His creatures for his goodness and the evildoer for his evil, not wronging any of them in anything, and accepting from them only Islam to Him and belief in Him. Then he related from Mujahid, through the chain of Shibl ibn Abi Najih from him, regarding ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56], that he said: "The truth." Likewise Ibn Jurayj narrated it from him.

Another group said: it is like His saying, ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]. This is a difference of expression, for His being ever watchful is the recompensing of the good-doer for his goodness and the evildoer for his evil.

Another group said: there is an omission in the speech, its implied meaning being: Indeed my Lord urges you upon a straight path and encourages you to it. As for these, if they intend that this is the meaning of the verse in question, then it is not as they claim, and there is no evidence for this implied elision. He, glorified is He, has distinguished between His being one who commands justice and His being on a straight path. If they intend that His urging to the straight path is among the entailments of His being on a straight path, then they are correct.

Another group said: the meaning of His being on a straight path is that the return of the servants and all affairs is to Allah, and nothing of them escapes Him. As for these, if they intend that this is the meaning of the verse, then it is not so; and if they intend that this is among the necessary consequences of His being on a straight path, and among its requirements and implications, then it is true.

Another group said: its meaning is that everything is under His power, subjugation, dominion and grip. This, although it is true, is not the meaning of the verse. Shu'ayb has distinguished between His saying, ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ [Hud: 56] and His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56], and so they are two independent meanings.

So the statement is the statement of Mujahid, and it is the view of the imams of tafsir. Arabic does not admit of any other reading except with strain. Jarir said, praising Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz:

"The Commander of the Faithful is upon a path, straight when the watering-places are crooked."

Allah, the Exalted, has said: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to misguide, He leaves him astray, and whomever He wills, He places him upon a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 39]. And since He, glorified is He, is the One who placed His messengers and their followers upon the straight path in their sayings and actions, He, glorified is He, is more deserving of being upon a straight path in His saying and His action. And although the path of the messengers and their followers is conformity with His command, His path upon which He is, is what His praise, perfection and glory require of the word of truth and of action. And success is from Allah.

(Section)

He informs of the generality of His power, the Exalted, and that all creation is under His subjugation and power, and that He holds their forelocks. So there is no escape for them from the execution of His will and power over them. Then He follows that with information about His disposal of them, that it is by justice and not by injustice, by goodness and not by evil, by righteousness and not by corruption. So He commands them and forbids them out of kindness toward them and as protection and safeguarding for them, not out of need for them, nor out of stinginess toward them, but out of generosity, bounty, benevolence and gentleness; and He rewards them out of goodness, favour and mercy, not in exchange for or as entitlement from them, nor as a debt obligatory upon Him that they are owed; and He punishes them out of justice and wisdom, not out of gloating, nor fear, nor injustice, as kings and others punish. Rather, He is upon the straight path, which is the path of justice and goodness, in His command and prohibition, His reward and His punishment.

So reflect upon the words of this verse and what it gathers of the generality of power, the perfection of dominion, the completeness of wisdom, justice and goodness, and what it contains of refutation of the two groups. Indeed it is among the treasures of the Qur'an. It suffices and heals for whoever has had the door of its understanding opened to him.

So His being exalted is on a straight path: it negates His wronging of the servants, and His imposing on them what they cannot bear. It negates defect from His actions and legislation, and establishes for them the utmost wisdom and soundness, as a refutation of those who deny this; and that every creature is under His grip and power, and He holds its forelock. It must be that no thing occurs in His dominion from any of His creatures without His will and power.

And that whoever has his forelock in the hand of Allah and in His grip cannot move except by His moving him, nor act except by His enabling him, nor will except by the will of Allah, the Exalted. This is the most eloquent refutation of those among the Qadariyya who deny this.

So the two groups did not fulfil the meaning of the verse, nor did they measure it by its true measure.

Thus He, glorified is He, is upon a straight path in His giving and withholding, His guidance and misguidance, in His benefit and harm, His well-being and trial, His enriching and impoverishing, His exalting and humbling, His bounty and vengeance, His reward and punishment, His giving life and causing death, His command and prohibition, His permitting and forbidding, and in all that He creates and all that He commands. And this knowledge of Allah is not attained except by the prophets and their heirs.

(Exhortation)

What does he own of his affair, the one whose forelock is in the hand of Allah, whose self is in His hand, whose heart is between two of His fingers, which He turns however He wills, whose life is in His hand, whose death is in His hand, whose happiness is in His hand, whose misery is in His hand, whose movements and stillnesses, sayings and deeds are by His permission and will? He does not move except by His permission, nor act except by His will. If He leaves him to himself, He leaves him to weakness, poverty, negligence, sin and error; and if He leaves him to another, He leaves him to one who does not possess for him harm or benefit, nor death, nor life, nor resurrection. And if He forsakes him, his enemy overpowers him and makes him his captive. So he has no independence from Him for the blink of an eye; rather he is in need of Him with every breath, in every atom of his being, inwardly and outwardly. His poverty toward Him is complete, and yet he turns away from Him and is averse to Him, displeasing Him by his disobedience, despite his utmost need for Him in every respect. He has become forgetful of His remembrance and has taken Him behind his back. Yet to Him is his return, and before Him is his standing.

(Section)

The sixteenth category: His, glorified is He, informing that He is upon a straight path in two places of His Book. The first is His saying, relating from His Prophet Hud: ﴿Indeed I have put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed my Lord is upon a straight path﴾

The second is His saying: ﴿Allah strikes a parable: two men, one of them mute, unable to do anything, a burden upon his master, wherever he directs him he brings no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice while he is upon a straight path?﴾ Abu Ishaq said: "He informed that, although His power reaches them by whatever He wills, He wills only justice."

Ibn al-Anbari said: "When He said 'except that He holds its forelock', it carried the meaning of 'it does not go out of His grip', the Subduer by His mighty dominion over every creature. Then He followed that with His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is upon a straight path﴾, meaning that He is upon the truth." He said: "This is like the speech of the Arabs when they describe a man of good conduct, justice and fairness; they say, 'His way is good,' though there is no path there." Other sayings were mentioned concerning the meaning of the verse, which are among the necessary consequences and effects of this meaning, such as the saying of some of them: "Indeed my Lord guides to a straight path," so His guiding to the path is among the requirements of His being upon a straight path in Himself, for that guidance and instruction are part of His mercy, goodness, justice and wisdom.

Some of them said: its meaning is that nothing is hidden from Him and no fugitive escapes from Him. Some of them said: the meaning is that there is no way for anyone and no path for him except through Him, like His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. This meaning is true, but that it is what is meant by the verse is not clear, for not all people travel the straight path such that it could be said they arrive at His travelling it. And when He intended this meaning, He said: ﴿To Us is their return﴾; ﴿Indeed to Us is their return﴾; ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾; ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾.

As for His, glorified is He, being described as upon a straight path, it is that He speaks the truth and does what is right. His words are true and just, all of His acts are right and good, and Allah speaks the truth and He guides to the way. So He says only what is praiseworthy, being truth, justice, truthfulness and wisdom in itself. This is well known in the speech of the Arabs. Jarir said, praising Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz:

"The Commander of the Faithful is upon a path, straight when the watering-places are crooked."

And when this is understood, it follows from His being upon a straight path that He does nothing except for a wisdom worthy of praise and an end more deserving of being willed than others. Thus His actions do not depart from wisdom, benefit, goodness, mercy, justice and rightness, just as His sayings do not depart from justice and truthfulness.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 66–67:

{فَلَمّا جاءَ أمْرُنا نَجَّيْنا صالِحًا والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ بِرَحْمَةٍ مِنّا ومِن خِزْيِ يَوْمِئِذٍ إنَّ رَبَّكَ هو القَوِيُّ العَزِيزُ (٦٦) وأخَذَ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا الصَّيْحَةُ فَأصْبَحُوا في دِيارِهِمْ جاثِمِينَ (٦٧)

فإذا قلت: فإذا استوى ذكر التاء وتركها في الفعل المتقدم وفاعله مؤنث غير حقيقي فما الحكمة في اختصاصها في قصة شعيب بالفعل وحذفها في قصة صالح {وأخذ الذين ظلموا الصيحة)؟

Qult: The Sayhah (the Cry) in the story of Salih carries the meaning of punishment and disgrace, since it is joined with His words: ﴿And from the disgrace of that day. Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty﴾. Thus the Sayhah becomes an expression for that disgrace and for the punishment mentioned in the verse, so the masculine form is strengthened. This is unlike the story of Shu'ayb, for nothing of that is mentioned there.

This is the answer of al-Suhayli.

But I have a better answer than this, God willing, which is: the Sayhah may be intended as a verbal noun in the sense of "crying out," in which case the masculine is good; and it may be intended as a single instance of the verbal noun, in which case the feminine is better. God Most High has informed us of the punishment that struck the people of Shu'ayb with three things, all feminine in form. The first is the Rajfah (the Quake), in His words in al-A'raf: ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became in their homes prostrate﴾.

The second is the Zullah (the Cloud), by His words: ﴿So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Cloud seized them﴾.

The third is the Sayhah: ﴿And those who had wronged were seized by the Sayhah﴾. He combined the three for them, for the Rajfah began with them, so they went out into the open plain fearing the collapse of the buildings upon them, and the sun scorched them with its heat, and the Cloud was raised over them, so they hastened toward it seeking shade from the sun. Then the punishment descended upon them from it, and in it was the Sayhah. Thus mentioning the Sayhah alongside the Rajfah and the Zullah is better than mentioning the cry, and mentioning the feminine ta' was (and God knows best).

If it is said: Why did you say that the ta' is a particle and did not treat it like the waw and alif in qama and qamu?

It is said: Because of the consensus of the Arabs on their saying "al-hindan qamatā" with the ta' and the pronoun, and it is not permissible for a verb to have two subject pronouns.

(Section)

As for the tenth question:

It concerns the secret behind the accusative (naṣb) in the greeting of Abraham's guests, the angels, and the nominative (rafʿ) in Abraham's greeting.

The answer: You have already learned the grammarians' view on this. The angels' greeting, "salāman," implies a verbal sentence, since the accusative of "salām" indicates "we greet you with a greeting" (salamnā ʿalayka salāman). Abraham's greeting, "salāmun," implies a nominal sentence, since its nominative indicates that the meaning is "peace be upon you" (salāmun ʿalaykum). A nominal sentence denotes permanence and fixity, whereas a verbal sentence denotes occurrence and renewal. Thus his greeting to them was more complete than theirs to him, and he had, in the rank of response, what befits his station, peace be upon him, namely the rank of excellence, for he greeted them with something better than their greeting. This is the statement of what they said.

But I have an answer to this better than that, namely that he did not intend to relate the angels' greeting. So "salāman" is in the accusative as the object of a simple verb of saying, as if it were said: "they said a saying, salām," and "they said a right and proper word," and the like. For the verb "qāla" (say) is only used to introduce whole sentences; a single word is not introduced by it, but is rather governed by it in the manner of a direct object.

From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Salām"﴾. The intention is not that they uttered this single word in the accusative; rather its meaning is "they said a saying, salām," like "sidādan" and "ṣawāban." The saying was called "salām" because it conveys the meaning of greeting and includes the removal of unease and the establishment of companionship.

He related the words of Abraham's greeting, so he gave them in his wording, in the nominative, as a subject of inception, quoted by the verb of saying. Had he not intended quotation, he would have said "salāman" in the accusative, because what follows "qāla," when it is nominative, is necessarily quotation. Thus the difference between the two utterances, in reporting Abraham's greeting with the nominative and the angels' with the accusative, points to a very subtle meaning: that the words "salāmun ʿalaykum" are from the religion of Islam, received from the leader of the ḥanīfs and father of the prophets, and that it is from the creed of Abraham, which God commanded and commanded us to follow. So He related his words so that emulation of him and following him might be achieved, and He did not relate the words of his guests, but reported them only in summary, not in detail. And God knows best. So weigh this answer and the previous one with an impartial scale, and the stronger of the two will become clear to you. And success is from God.

(Benefit: that the one who was sacrificed was Isma'il, peace be upon him, and not Isaac)

How could it be proper to say that the one who was sacrificed was Isaac, when Allah Most High had already given glad tidings to Isaac's mother of him and of his son Ya'qub? Allah Most High said, concerning the angels, that when they came to Ibrahim with the glad tidings, they said: ﴿Fear not. We have been sent to the people of Lut.﴾ And his wife was standing, so she laughed, and We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Ya'qub.

It is impossible that he would give her the glad tidings that a son would be born to her and then command that he be slaughtered. And there is no doubt that Ya'qub, may Allah be pleased with him, is included in the glad tidings. So the glad tidings' reference to Isaac and Ya'qub in the wording is one, and this is the apparent meaning of the speech and its context.

Also, Allah, glory be to Him, gave glad tidings to Sarah, the mother of Isaac: ﴿of Isaac, and after Isaac, Ya'qub﴾

So He gave her glad tidings of both of them together. How, then, would He command, after that, the slaughter of Isaac, when He had already given his parents glad tidings of their son's son?!

If it is said: "If the matter were as you have mentioned, 'Ya'qub' would be in the genitive as a conjunction with Isaac, and the reading would be ﴿wa-min wara'i Ishaqa Ya'quba﴾"

That is: "and Ya'qub from behind Isaac."

It is said: The nominative does not prevent Ya'qub from being the one given glad tidings of, because glad tidings is a specific kind of speech, and it is the first truthful report of good news. And His saying, Most High: ﴿and after Isaac, Ya'qub﴾ is a sentence containing these qualifications, so it is glad tidings. Indeed, the true nature of glad tidings is the declarative sentence itself.

Since glad tidings is speech, the position of this sentence is in the accusative by way of reporting speech, as if the meaning were: "And We said to her: after Isaac, Ya'qub will come." When the speaker says, "I gave so-and-so the glad tidings of the arrival of his brother and his baggage following him," nothing is understood from it except the glad tidings of both matters together. No person of understanding has any doubt about this at all. Then another matter weakens the genitive reading: the weakness of your saying, "I passed by Zayd and after him 'Amr," and because the conjunction takes the place of the preposition, it is not separated from the genitive noun, just as the preposition is not separated from the noun it governs.

(Excellent section: on concluding the prayer upon the Prophet ﷺ with these two names of the Lord, may He be glorified and exalted, namely al-Ḥamīd and al-Majīd.)

Al-Ḥamīd is on the pattern fa'īl from al-ḥamd (praise), and it means maḥmūd (praised). Most of the divine names in the fa'īl pattern carry the meaning of the active participle (fā'il), such as Samī' (All-Hearing), Baṣīr (All-Seeing), ʿAlīm (All-Knowing), Qadīr (All-Powerful), ʿAlī (Most High), Ḥakīm (All-Wise), and Ḥalīm (Most Forbearing). This is common. Likewise the pattern fa'ūl, as in Ghafūr (Most Forgiving), Shakūr (Most Appreciative), and Ṣabūr (Most Patient).

As for al-Wadūd, there are two opinions:

The first is that it carries the meaning of the active participle (fā'il), namely the One who loves His prophets, messengers, friends, and the believing servants.

The second is that it carries the meaning of the passive participle (mafʿūl, i.e., mawdūd), namely the Beloved who deserves to be loved with all love and to be dearer to the servant than his hearing, his sight, and all that he loves.

As for al-Ḥamīd, it comes only in the meaning of maḥmūd, and it is more emphatic than maḥmūd. When fa'īl is used in place of maf'ūl, it indicates that the quality has become like a disposition, an innate nature, and a settled character, as when you say: fulān ẓarīf (refined), sharīf (noble), and karīm (generous). For this reason this form is generally derived from verbs of the pattern sharufa, the form of innate and inherent dispositions, such as kabura (to be great), ṣaghura (to be small), ḥasuna (to be beautiful), luṭufa (to be gentle), and similar.

For this reason ḥabīb is more emphatic than maḥbūb. The ḥabīb is one in whom the qualities and actions for which he is loved are present, so he is beloved in himself, even if others do not love him because they are unaware of him or because something prevents them from loving him. The maḥbūb, on the other hand, is one upon whom the love of a lover has fallen, so he becomes beloved through the love of another. The ḥabīb is beloved by his very essence and attributes, whether or not another's love attaches to him. The same holds for ḥamīd and maḥmūd.

Thus al-Ḥamīd is He who possesses the qualities and causes of praise that necessitate that He be praised, even if no one else praises Him; He is praiseworthy in Himself. The maḥmūd is one upon whom the praise of those who praise has fallen. Likewise al-Majīd, al-Mumajjad, al-Kabīr, al-Mukabbir, al-ʿAẓīm, and al-Mu'aẓẓam.

Praise (ḥamd) and glory (majd) both return to all perfection. Praise necessitates commendation and love for the one praised. Whoever you love but do not commend, you have not praised, until you both commend him and love him. This commendation and love follow the causes that necessitate them, namely the attributes of perfection, the qualities of majesty, and the benefaction to others that the praised one possesses. These are the causes of love, and the more comprehensive and perfect these attributes are, the more complete and great the praise and love become. God, glory be to Him, has absolute perfection, with no deficiency in any respect, and all benefaction is His and from Him. Therefore He is most worthy of all praise and all love from every standpoint. He deserves to be loved for His essence, His attributes, His actions, His names, His benefaction, and everything that proceeds from Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

As for majd, it necessitates greatness, vastness, and majesty, and praise indicates the attributes of honor. God, glory be to Him and exalted, is ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honor﴾. This is the meaning of the servant's saying: "There is no god but God, and God is greatest." "There is no god but God" indicates His divinity and His singularity in it, and His divinity necessitates complete love for Him. "God is greatest" indicates His glory and His greatness, and this necessitates magnifying Him, glorifying Him, and proclaiming His greatness. For this reason, glory be to Him, He frequently joins these two categories in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house; indeed He is Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾ [Hud 11:73].

And His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And say: Praise be to God, who has not taken a son, and has had no partner in the dominion, nor any protector out of weakness; and magnify Him with full magnification﴾ [al-Isra' 17:111]. So He commanded praise of Himself and the proclaiming of His greatness.

And He said, exalted be He: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman 55:78].

And He said, exalted be He: ﴿And there remains the face of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honor﴾ [al-Rahman 55:27].

In al-Musnad and Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān and others, from the ḥadīth of Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Persist in invoking Dhū al-Jalāl wal-Ikrām" — a ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīth, meaning: hold fast to it and cling to it. So "al-Jalāl wal-Ikrām" is praise and glory. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous﴾ [al-Naml 27:40].

And His saying: ﴿Indeed God was ever Pardoner, Able﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:149].

And His saying: ﴿And God is Able, God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:7].

And His saying: ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Possessor of the Throne, the Glorious﴾ [al-Buruj 85:14-15].

This is frequent in the Qur'an.

In the authentic ḥadīth of the supplication of distress (duʿā' al-karb): "There is no god but God, the Mighty, the Forbearing. There is no god but God, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but God, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth and Lord of the Noble Throne." Here he mentioned these two names, al-Ḥamīd and al-Majīd, after the prayer upon the Prophet ﷺ and upon his family, in agreement with His saying: ﴿The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house; indeed He is Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾ [Hud 11:73].

Since the prayer upon the Prophet ﷺ, which is God's praise of him, His honoring him, His elevating his mention, increasing His love for him, and bringing him near, as has preceded, includes praise and glory, it is as if the one praying asks God, exalted be He, to increase His praise and glory. The prayer upon him is a kind of praise of Him and glorification of Him; this is its reality. So he mentioned in this request the two names fitting to it, namely al-Ḥamīd and al-Majīd. This is as has preceded: the supplicant is prescribed to conclude his supplication with one of the Most Beautiful Names suited to his request, or to open his supplication with it, and it has preceded that this is from His saying: ﴿And to God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf 7:180]. Sulayman, peace be upon him, said in his supplication to his Lord: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and grant me a dominion that will not belong to anyone after me; indeed You are the Bestower﴾ [Sad 38:35].

And al-Khalil (Abraham) and his son Isma'il, peace be upon them, said in their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, make us submissive to You, and of our descendants a community submissive to You, and show us our rites and turn to us; indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:128].

The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "My Lord, forgive me and accept my repentance; indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Forgiving," one hundred times in his sitting. [Its chain is ṣaḥīḥ.]

He ﷺ also said to ʿĀ'ishah, may God be pleased with her, when she asked him what to supplicate if she happened upon the Night of Power: "Say: O God, You are Pardoning and You love pardon, so pardon me." [Its chain is ṣaḥīḥ.]

He ﷺ also said to al-Ṣiddīq, may God be pleased with him, when he asked him to teach him a supplication to recite in his prayer: "Say: O God, I have wronged myself greatly, and none forgives sins but You. So forgive me a forgiveness from Yourself, and have mercy on me; indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful." This is abundant, and we have mentioned it in the book al-Rūḥ wal-Nafs.

As for what people have said regarding the words of Christ ﷺ: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾, he did not say "the Forgiving, the Merciful."

And the words of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim 14:36].

Since what the Messenger ﷺ sought was praise and glory through God's prayer upon him, he concluded this request with the two names al-Ḥamīd and al-Majīd. Also, since what the Messenger sought was praise and glory, and that was already his, he concluded it with an affirmation that these two attributes belong to the Lord, by way of priority, since every perfection in the servant does not necessitate deficiency, and the Lord is more worthy of it.

Also, since he sought praise and glory for the Messenger through the prayer upon him, which necessitates commendation of him, he concluded this request with commendation of the One who sent him with praise and glory. Thus this supplication includes a request for praise and glory for the Messenger ﷺ and an affirmation of their being the attributes of the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 78:

The statement of Lot to his people: ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾

He gathers several kinds of appeal to their compassion:

The first: addressing them with the address of a sincere and compassionate advisor, with his words ﴿O my people﴾, and he did not say "O these people."

The second: presenting his daughters to them with his words ﴿these are my daughters﴾.

The third: making that concrete by pointing with a word of presence (hā' al-tanbīh, "these").

The fourth: encouraging them toward them because of their purity and goodness.

The fifth: reminding them of Allah the Exalted with his words ﴿so fear Allah﴾.

The sixth: demanding the preservation of protection and the abandoning of harm with his words ﴿and do not disgrace me﴾.

The seventh: severe reproach with his words ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verses 79–83:

{And there came to him his people, rushing toward him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of right judgment?" (78) They said, "You already know that we have no need of your daughters, and indeed you know what we want." (79) He said, "If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a strong support." (80) They said, "O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; indeed, what will strike them will strike her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?" (81) So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of hard clay, layered, (82) marked from your Lord. And it is not far from the wrongdoers." (83)

Contemplate the vileness of the people of Lot and the extremes of their rebellion against Allah, when they came to their prophet Lot after hearing that guests had come to him, guests who were among the most beautiful of people in appearance. The people of Lot came hurrying toward them, and when he saw them he said to them: ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾ [Hud: 78].

He offered his daughters to ransom his guests, to marry them to them, out of fear for himself and his guests from the severe shame, and he said: ﴿O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of right judgment?﴾ They answered him, but with the response of a tyrannical, obstinate one: ﴿You already know that we have no need of your daughters, and indeed you know what we want﴾ [Hud: 79].

The prophet of Allah then breathed out a breath of one who is burdened, coming from a distressed heart, and said: ﴿If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a strong support﴾. The messengers of Allah then relieved him regarding the reality of the situation, and informed him that they were of those who could not be reached, nor could he be reached through them. So do not fear them, do not concern yourself with them, and ease your mind. They said: ﴿O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾, and they gave him good news of what they had come with, the promise to him and the striking threat against his people. They said: ﴿So set out with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; indeed, what will strike them will strike her. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?﴾ [Hud: 81].

The prophet of Allah was slow to see the appointed time of their destruction, and said: "I want it sooner than this." The angels said: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾. By Allah, the gap between the destruction of the enemies of Allah and the deliverance of His prophet and His allies was no more than the span between the pre-dawn and the rising of dawn. Suddenly their dwellings were uprooted from their foundations and lifted toward the sky, until the angels heard the barking of dogs and the braying of donkeys. Then the decree that cannot be turned back went forth from the Lord, the Majestic, to His servant and messenger Gabriel, to overturn it upon them as He had told in the well-guarded revelation. So the Mighty, the One who speaks said: ﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of hard clay, layered﴾ [Hud: 82]. Thus He made them a sign for the worlds, an admonition for the God-fearing, a punishment and a warning for whoever shared their deeds among the criminals, and He made their dwellings a path for travelers: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern - and indeed it is on a road that remains. Indeed in that is a sign for the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 75–77].

He seized them unawares while they were asleep, and His punishment came to them while they were in their intoxication, wandering blindly, and what they had earned did not avail them. So that pleasure turned into pains, and they became tormented by it.

Desires that were in life for their people / became a torment, and in death became a torment.

Pleasures passed away and brought regrets, the lusts ended, and they bequeathed wretchedness. They enjoyed for a little while and were tormented for a long time. They grazed in a pasture of ruin, so it brought them a painful punishment. The wine of those lusts intoxicated them, and they did not awaken from it except in the dwellings of the tormented. That heedlessness lulled them to sleep, and they did not awaken from it except while they were in the abodes of the ruined. They regretted, by Allah, with the most intense regret, when regret no longer benefits, and they wept over what they had sent ahead, with blood instead of tears. If you had seen the high and the low of this group, with fire coming out of the openings of their faces and bodies, while they were between the layers of hellfire, drinking boiling water instead of the sweet drink, and it is said to them while they are being dragged on their faces: ﴿Taste what you used to earn. Burn in it, so be patient or be not patient; it is all the same for you. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ [al-Tur: 16].

Allah, glorified is He, has brought the distance of punishment close between this nation and their brothers in deed, and He said, warning them lest the threat befall them: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud: 83].

Oh you who marry males, may the good news bring you joy, for on the Day of the gathering of people you will have a reward.

Eat, drink, commit fornication, and be joyful, for you have a rush toward the red Paradise.

Your brothers have already prepared the abode before you, and said: "Hasten to us, the good news is for you."

And here we are, your forerunners, awaiting you.

The Almighty will gather us in His great fire. Do not think that those you have married

will be hidden from you, rather you will see them plainly.

Each of you will curse his companion, and the sorrowful one will suffer in the next return.

He punishes each of you by his partner, as the two shared in a pleasure that brings sin.

(Section)
