When the soul becomes free, good, and at peace, enriched by what its Owner and Originator has enriched it with, namely the light that has settled in the heart and overflowed from it to the soul, it stays steadfast by that richness upon the command that was bestowed, is kept by it from what is displeasing, and is freed from showing off. All of this revolves around steadfastness, inwardly and outwardly. For this reason the whole of religion is contained in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded.﴾

(Principle: on mentioning a path that leads to steadfastness in states, speech and deeds)

It consists of two things:

The first: guarding and protecting the thoughts (khawatir, sing. khatir: passing thoughts), being wary of neglecting them and of drifting along with them, for the root of all corruption comes from them, since they are the seed of Satan, and the soul is in the earth of the heart. When his seed takes root, Satan tends it by watering it again and again until it becomes desires (iradat), then he keeps watering it until it becomes resolves (aza'im), then he does not cease with it until it bears deeds. There is no doubt that repelling thoughts is easier than repelling desires and resolves. So the servant finds himself unable, or as one who is unable, to repel them once they have become a firm desire. He who is negligent is the one who does not repel them while they are weak passing thoughts, like one who disregards a spark of fire that falls on dry wood: once it has taken hold, he is unable to extinguish it.

If you ask: what is the way to guard the thoughts?

I say: there are several means.

The first: the certain knowledge that the Lord, Exalted is He, watches over your heart, and knows the details of your thoughts.

The second: your modesty (haya') before Him.

The third: your reverence for Him, that He should see such thoughts in His house, which He created for knowing Him and loving Him.

The fourth: your fear that you may fall from His sight because of those thoughts.

The fifth: your preference for Him, that you would not let anything other than His love dwell in your heart.

The sixth: your fear that those thoughts, if they arise, their sparks will blaze and consume the faith and love of God that are in the heart, so that they take it away entirely while you do not perceive it.

The seventh: that you know those thoughts are like the grain thrown to a bird in order to hunt it. Know that every one of them is a grain in a snare set for your catching, while you do not perceive it.

The eighth: that you know those base thoughts never gather together with the thoughts of faith and the motives of love and turning back (to God), not at all; rather they are its opposite in every respect. Those two never meet in one heart without one of them overcoming the other, expelling it and settling in its place. So what is to be thought of a heart in which the thoughts of the soul and of Satan have overcome the thoughts of faith, knowledge and love, expelling them and settling in their place? Yet if the heart had life, it would feel the pain of that and perceive its calamity.

The ninth: that he knows those thoughts are a sea of imaginings without shore. When the heart enters its depths, it drowns in them and wanders lost in its darkness, seeking deliverance but finding no way to it. A heart possessed by thoughts is far from success, tormented, and busied with what benefits nothing.

The tenth: that those thoughts are the valley of fools and the wishful thinking of the ignorant. They bear for their owner nothing but regret and disgrace. When they overcome the heart, they bring it whisperings, remove it from its own authority, corrupt its subjects against it, and cast it into long captivity. Just as this is known of the thoughts of the soul, so too the thoughts of faith and the Merciful are the root of all good. When the earth of the heart is sown with thoughts of faith, fear (of God), love, turning back, belief in the promise and hope for reward, and they are watered again and again, and their owner tends them by guarding and caring for them, they bear for him every beautiful deed, fill his heart with goodness, employ his limbs in acts of obedience, the king is established in his dominion by them, and his subjects are set right for him. For this reason, when a group of the wayfarers realized this, they worked to guard the thoughts, and that became their journey and the bulk of their work. This is beneficial to its practitioner on two conditions. The first: that he does not thereby abandon an obligation or a sunnah. The second: that he does not make the mere guarding of them the goal; rather, it is not complete unless he places in their stead thoughts of faith, love, turning back, trust (tawakkul) and fear (of God), emptying his heart of those thoughts and filling it with their opposites. Otherwise, if he works only at emptying it of them, he is a loser. So one must be alert to this.

From here, some people among the masters of the path erred, and they worked to cast out the thoughts and remove them entirely. So Satan sowed in them kinds of doubts and imaginings, and they took these to be verification and a divine opening, while they were deluded in this; these were only satanic imaginings and satanic openings. The criterion is the Speaking Book, the sound nature, and reason supported by the light of prophecy. And God is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 11, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have done wrong﴾

Imam Ahmad said: "Do not approve of their deeds."

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 11, verse 114:

«A man asked him (ﷺ), saying: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about a man who met a woman whom he did not know, and there is nothing a man does with his wife except that he has done it with her, except that he did not have intercourse with her? So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds.﴾ [Hud: 114]."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Perform ablution, then pray." Mu'adh said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, is this for him specifically, or for the believers in general?'"

He said: "Rather, it is for the believers in general."»

And in another narration:

«A man asked him (ﷺ), saying: "I kissed a woman," so this was revealed: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ [Hud: 114]. The man said: "Is this for me?" He said: "Rather, it is for whoever among my ummah acts upon it."» Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh).

Some have used this hadith to argue that ta'zir (discretionary punishment, imposed by the judge at his discretion) is not obligatory, and that the ruler (imam) may waive it. There is no evidence for this in it, so reflect upon it.

[Section on Strangeness (Faṣl al-Ghurba)]

Shaykh al-Islam said: Chapter on Strangeness (al-ghurba). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you those of remaining virtue who forbade corruption on earth, except a few of those We saved from among them?﴾ [Hud: 116].

His citing this verse in this chapter indicates his firm grounding in knowledge, understanding and comprehension of the Qur'an. For the strangers in the world are the people of this description mentioned in the verse, and they are those whom the Prophet ﷺ referred to in his saying: "Islam began as something strange, and it will return to being strange as it began. So blessed are the strangers." It was said: "Who are the strangers, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Those who set things right when people have become corrupt."

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, from Zuhayr ibn Amr ibn Abi Amr, client of al-Muttalib ibn Hantab, from al-Muttalib ibn Hantab, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Blessed are the strangers." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are the strangers?" He said: "Those who increase [in goodness] when people decrease."

If this hadith with this wording is preserved, its wording was not reversed for the narrator, namely: "Those who decrease when people increase," then its meaning is: those who increase in goodness, faith and piety when people decrease in that. And Allah knows best.

In the hadith of al-A'mash, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Islam began as something strange, and it will return to being strange as it began, so blessed are the strangers." It was said: "Who are the strangers, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "The ones who pull away from the tribes."

In the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ said one day while we were with him: 'Blessed are the strangers.' It was said: 'Who are the strangers, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Righteous people, few among many people; those who disobey them are more numerous than those who obey them.'"

Ahmad also said: al-Haytham ibn Jamil related to us, Muhammad ibn Muslim related to us, Uthman ibn Abdullah related to us, from Sulayman ibn Hurmuz, from Abdullah ibn Amr, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Indeed the most beloved thing to Allah is the strangers." It was said: "Who are the strangers?" He said: "Those who flee with their religion, gathering to Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, on the Day of Resurrection."

In another hadith: "Islam began as something strange, and it will return to being strange as it began, so blessed are the strangers." It was said: "Who are the strangers, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Those who revive my Sunnah and teach it to the people."

Nafi' related from Malik: Umar ibn al-Khattab entered the mosque and found Mu'adh ibn Jabal sitting by the house of the Prophet ﷺ, weeping. Umar said to him: "What makes you weep, Abu Abd al-Rahman? Has your brother died?" He said: "No, but a hadith my beloved ﷺ related to me while I was in this mosque." He said: "What is it?" He said: "Indeed Allah loves the unobtrusive, the devout, the pious, the innocent, those who when they are absent are not missed, and when they are present are not recognized; their hearts are lamps of guidance, they emerge from every dark, blind trial."

These are the praiseworthy strangers, envied, and because of their great rarity among people they were called strangers, for most people are not upon these qualities. So the people of Islam are strangers among people, the believers are strangers among the people of Islam, and the people of knowledge are strangers among the believers.

The People of the Sunnah, who distinguish it from desires and innovations, are strangers; and those who call to it, patient over the harm of its opponents, are the most intensely strange of these. Yet these are truly the People of Allah, so there is no strangeness upon them; their strangeness is only among the majority, of whom Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 116]. Those are the strangers from Allah, His Messenger and His religion, and their strangeness is the lonely strangeness, even if they are the well-known ones pointed to, as it is said:

"He is not a stranger whose home is far away, / but the stranger is one from whom those close to him have turned away."

When Musa, peace be upon him, fled from the people of Pharaoh and arrived at Madyan in the state Allah mentioned, lonely, strange, fearful and hungry, he said: "My Lord, a lonely, sick stranger." It was said to him: "O Musa, the lonely one is one who has no companion like Me; the sick one is one who has no physician like Me; the stranger is one with whom I have no dealings."

[Types of Strangeness]

[The First: the strangeness of the People of Allah and the People of the Sunnah of His Messenger among this creation]

Strangeness is of three types. The first: the strangeness of the People of Allah and the People of the Sunnah of His Messenger among this creation, which is the strangeness whose people the Messenger of Allah ﷺ praised, and he informed about the religion he brought: that it began strange, that it will return strange as it began, and that its people will become strangers.

This strangeness may occur in one place and not another, one time and not another, among one people and not another; but the people of this strangeness are truly the People of Allah, for they have not taken refuge in other than Allah, have not ascribed themselves to other than His Messenger ﷺ, and have not called to other than what he brought. They are those who parted from people when they most needed them. When people set off on the Day of Resurrection with their gods, they remain in their place, and it is said to them: "Will you not set off where the people have set off?" They say: "We parted from the people while we were more in need of them today than they are of us, and we await our Lord whom we used to worship."

For this strangeness brings no loneliness upon its bearer; rather, he is most at ease when people are lonely, and his loneliness is most intense when they are at ease. His Walī is Allah, His Messenger and the believers, even if most people oppose him and shun him.

In the hadith of al-Qasim, from Abu Umama, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said, from Allah the Exalted: "Indeed the most envied of My friends in My sight is a believer, light in his burden, with a share of his prayer, who worshipped his Lord well, whose provision was sufficient, who was obscure among people, not pointed at with fingers, and who was patient in that until he met Allah; then his death came, his inheritance was small, and few were those who wept for him."

Among these strangers is the one mentioned by Anas in his hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: "Many a dishevelled, dust-covered one, with two worn garments, who is not regarded, who if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfil it for him."

In the hadith of Abu Idris al-Khawlani, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Shall I not inform you about the kings of the people of Paradise?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Every weak, dust-covered one with two worn garments, who is not regarded, who if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfil it for him." Al-Hasan said: The believer in this world is like a stranger; he does not grieve at its humiliation, nor vie for its honour. For people there is a state, and for him there is a state; people are at ease from him, while he is in toil from himself.

When a believer whom Allah has granted insight into his religion, understanding of the Sunnah of His Messenger, and comprehension of His Book, and has shown him what people are engaged in of desires, innovations and misguidance, and their deviation from the Straight Path upon which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions were, then if he wishes to tread this path, let him prepare himself for the disparagement of the ignorant and the people of innovation regarding it, their criticism of it, their disparagement of it, their repelling of people from it and warning them against it, just as their predecessors among the disbelievers did with the one they followed and imam, ﷺ. As for if he calls them to that and criticises what they are upon, then there their resurrection arises: they seek to harm him, set snares for him, and bring against him their cavalry and infantry, big and small.

He is a stranger in his religion because of the corruption of their religions; a stranger in his adherence to the Sunnah because of their adherence to innovations; a stranger in his creed because of the corruption of their creeds; a stranger in his prayer because of the badness of their prayers; a stranger in his path because of the misguidance and corruption of their paths; a stranger in his lineage because of the opposition of their lineage; a stranger in his companionship with them, because he keeps company with them in what their souls do not desire.

In summary: he is a stranger in the affairs of his worldly life and his hereafter; he finds from the common folk no supporter or helper. He is a scholar among ignorant people, a bearer of the Sunnah among people of innovation, a caller to Allah and His Messenger among callers to desires and innovations, one who enjoins good and forbids evil among a people for whom the good is reprehensible and the evil is good.

[Section: The Second, the strangeness of the People of Falsehood]

The second type of strangeness is a blameworthy strangeness: the strangeness of the People of Falsehood and the People of Immorality among the People of Truth. It is a strangeness among the party of Allah, the successful, even if its adherents are many; they are strangers despite the multitude of their companions and followers, people of loneliness despite the abundance of their companions. They are known among the people of the earth, and hidden from the people of heaven.

[Section: The Third, a shared strangeness that is neither praised nor blamed]

This is the strangeness from one's homeland. Indeed all people in this abode are strangers, for it is not a dwelling of permanence for them, nor is it the abode for which they were created. The Prophet ﷺ said to Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveller along the way." And so it is in reality, for he is commanded to contemplate this with his heart and to know it with true knowledge. I have some verses on this meaning:

"Come to the Gardens of Eden, for they / are your first abodes, and therein is the resting place."

"But we are captives of the enemy; will we ever see / our homelands again, and be safe?"

"What estrangement is greater than our estrangement, / for which the enemies have come to rule over us?"

"They claim that the stranger, when he is far away / and his homelands have receded from him, does not find ease."

"Therefore the servant does not enjoy an hour / of his life except after he has suffered."

And how could the servant not be a stranger in this abode, when he is upon the wing of a journey, dismounting from his mount only among the people of graves? He is a traveller in the form of one who sits. It has been said:

"These days are but stages, / driven by a summoner to death, heading toward it."

"And the most wondrous thing, if you reflect, is that / they are dwellings that are folded up, while the traveller sits."

There are two opinions regarding the verse. The first is: "He would not destroy them for an injustice committed by them." The second is: "He would not destroy them for an injustice committed by Him."

According to the first opinion, the meaning is: He would not destroy them for their earlier injustice while they are now reformers. That is, after they have reformed and repented, He would not destroy them for the injustice that had preceded from them.

According to the second opinion, He was not unjust to them in destroying them, for He did not destroy them while they were reformers. Rather, He destroyed them while they were wrongdoers. They are the wrongdoers because of their opposition, and He is the just one in destroying them. The two opinions also apply to the verse in Surat al-An'am: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people are unaware﴾ [al-An'am: 131].

Ibn 'Abbas, Malik, and a group of the early generation (al-Salaf) said regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them﴾.

They said: He created the people of mercy for mercy, and the people of difference for difference.

Ibn 'Abbas, Malik, and a group of the early generation (al-Salaf) said regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them﴾.

They said: He created the people of mercy for mercy, and the people of difference for difference.
